cases.prompt: Write 350–450 words explaining database isolation to an experienced engineer. Use sections for serializable transactions, snapshot isolation, a concrete two-doctor on-call write-skew example, and mitigation. Preserve: serializable outcomes are equivalent to serial execution; snapshot isolation can permit write skew when concurrent transactions read a shared constraint and update disjoint rows; both doctors can go off call, violating the at-least-one-doctor rule. Explain how serializable isolation can abort a conflicting transaction and why the application must retry the entire transaction. Do not replace the requested depth with a short summary.

pass:
Serializable transactions
Serializable transactions produce outcomes equivalent to some serial execution. Transactions can still overlap in time; the guarantee concerns their combined observable result. A successful set of transactions must behave as though they ran one after another in some order. This property makes cross-row business rules easier to reason about when each transaction checks the rule before making its change. It does not mean that every implementation literally runs transactions one at a time.

Snapshot isolation
Snapshot isolation gives a transaction a consistent view of committed data. It can prevent transactions from observing another transaction's partly completed work. However, snapshot isolation can permit write skew when concurrent transactions read a shared constraint and update disjoint rows. Each transaction can make a locally reasonable decision from its snapshot, yet the combined committed result can break the rule. A consistent read view alone is not the same guarantee as serializability.

Two-doctor example
Suppose Alice and Ben are both on call. At least one of two doctors must remain on call. Alice's transaction reads both rows and sees Ben on call. Ben's transaction reads both rows and sees Alice on call. Alice updates her own row to go off call, while Ben updates his own row to do the same. The updates affect different rows, so checking only direct write conflicts need not reject either change. Now neither doctor is on call, even though each transaction checked that another doctor was available. There is no serial order of those two successful decisions that preserves the checks and produces that result.

Mitigation
Serializable isolation can detect the conflicting dependency pattern and abort a conflicting transaction instead of allowing both decisions to commit. The application must retry the entire transaction, including the reads and the constraint check, because the original decision used a snapshot that is no longer a valid basis for that transaction. Retrying only the final update would preserve the stale decision rather than recomputing it. After one doctor's change commits, the retried transaction can observe that no other doctor remains on call and refuse the second change. Application error handling must distinguish a retryable serialization failure from an unrelated failure; successful execution still depends on implementing the business check correctly.
